title: He Began as a Net Bowler for Mumbai Indians. In Dharamsala, Gurnoor Brar Took Three Wickets on Debut.
excerpt: The 6'5" Punjab pacer, fast-tracked for the 2027 World Cup, dismissed Ibrahim Zadran with his fifth ball in international cricket and finished with 3 for 27.
body:
Gurnoor Brar's journey to international cricket began in the most unglamorous way imaginable. Before he was a Punjab domestic cricketer, before Gujarat Titans signed him, and long before he stood at the top of his mark in Dharamsala with an India cap on his head, he was a net bowler at Mumbai Indians — running in, over after over, for batters who barely noticed him.

On Saturday, in the first ODI of India's three-match series against Afghanistan, the 26-year-old pacer from Muktsar announced himself to the cricketing world with figures of 3 for 27 in 4.5 overs, consistently bowling above 145 kmph and generating the kind of steep bounce that only someone standing 6 feet 5 inches tall can extract.

Wicket on the Fifth Ball

Brar needed just five deliveries in international cricket to claim his maiden wicket. Bowling the second over of Afghanistan's innings, he produced a teasing length ball that moved away late off the surface. Ibrahim Zadran, the visitors' opener, went for a drive but only managed a leading edge that carried to captain Shubman Gill at mid-off.

"It's a special feeling, like all the hard work finally paid off," Brar told BCCI.tv after the match. "All the grind, like I did in this heat, and in winter especially. It's a special moment."

He closed out Afghanistan's innings in equally emphatic fashion, picking up two more wickets — Rashid Khan and Zia-ur-Rehman — in the final over as the visitors were bundled out for 194 in a rain-curtailed 25-over contest.

The Making of a Fast Bowler

The path from Muktsar, a district in southern Punjab known more for its mustard fields than its cricket pitches, to international debut is not a well-worn one. Brar's breakthrough came in the 2024-25 Ranji Trophy season, when he took 26 wickets in seven matches to finish as Punjab's leading wicket-taker. That same year, he topped the wicket-takers' chart in the Sher-E-Punjab T20 with 22 wickets in 11 matches at an average of 14.

Gujarat Titans picked him up at the 2025 IPL mega auction for INR 1.30 crore, placing him under the coaching of former India pacer Ashish Nehra. The investment reflected a bet on physical attributes and raw pace that Indian cricket rarely produces — a bowler who can hit the deck hard, generate uncomfortable bounce on flat wickets, and bowl consistently in the 145-150 kmph range.

India's bowling coach Morne Morkel, himself a towering fast bowler who understood the value of height and hit-the-deck bowling, praised the new generation after the match. "My initial thoughts were that they seemed like they had been part of the team for years," Morkel said. "There was no sign of nervousness."

Fast-Tracked for a Reason

Former India opener Wasim Jaffer offered perhaps the most telling assessment. "He has been fast-tracked because of his pace, his speed, and his height," Jaffer said on his YouTube channel. "He bowls at speeds of 144-145 kmph, gets bounce, and has a very good, solid, strong action. He has not played a lot of junior cricket. I feel the more he plays, the better he will become."

The numbers bear out just how unusual Brar's elevation has been. He had played only 10 List A matches before receiving his ODI cap — presented by KL Rahul before the match in Dharamsala. In an era where Indian fast bowlers typically spend years grinding through domestic cricket and India A tours before earning international recognition, Brar's ascent has been unusually swift. Chief selector Ajit Agarkar has made no secret of the fact that Brar is being groomed with the 2027 ODI World Cup in South Africa firmly in mind.

The Bigger Picture

Brar was not the only debutant in Dharamsala. Harsh Dubey, a 25-year-old left-arm spin-bowling all-rounder, also received his maiden ODI cap, presented by Gill. Together, they represent India's deliberate strategy of blooding young talent against touring sides to build depth ahead of the next World Cup cycle.

The match itself was a comfortable affair for India. After restricting Afghanistan to 194, Gill anchored the chase with an unbeaten 84 off 66 balls, supported by Ishan Kishan (34) and KL Rahul (39 not out off 19 balls). India won by seven wickets with 13 balls remaining.

The two teams now travel to Lucknow for the second ODI on June 17, before concluding the series in Chennai on June 20. For Brar, the immediate challenge is simple: replicate Dharamsala's promise on wickets that will offer far less for the seamers.

What NRIs Should Watch

For diaspora cricket fans who track the pipeline beyond the headliners, Brar is exactly the kind of prospect worth watching. India have historically struggled to produce fast bowlers who can extract bounce on flat, slow wickets abroad — the surfaces they will encounter at the 2027 World Cup in South Africa. At 6'5" with genuine pace, Brar offers something that the Indian attack has lacked since Ishant Sharma's peak years. If his development continues at this pace, he could be a name on the team sheet in Johannesburg and Cape Town next year.
